playfield.note: MAME galaga.cpp:1508 set_raw plus the driver’s ROT90 — a 224-wide by 288-tall portrait raster. Arcade reference section 2.

lives.default.note: Switch-selectable 2, 3, 4 or 5 fighters; the factory default is 3.

lives.options.note: The four settings the cabinet offers.

extraLives.award.note: Setting 1 of the 2/3/4-fighter table — 20,000, then 70,000, then every 70,000. Operator manual and MAME’s dipswitch block.

extraLives.setting.note: The DIP setting the cabinet shipped on, for both threshold tables.

extraLives.options.note: Both threshold tables, eight settings each: one set for a 2-, 3- or 4-fighter cabinet and a different set for a 5-fighter one. The available thresholds depend on the starting-fighter count, so one table keyed by setting alone awards the wrong bonuses.

extraLives.thresholdUnit.note: The bonus check reads two score digits and compares floor(score / 10,000) mod 100 with the pending threshold, which is carried in the same units of 10,000. Arcade reference section 3, the tail of `gctl_supv_score`.

extraLives.thresholdModulus.note: Two digits, so a threshold that reaches 100 can never match and the awards stop: with the factory default they run 2, 7, 14 … 98 and then 105, making 980,000 the last extra life (960,000 on a 5-fighter cabinet). The score itself does not roll over there. Arcade reference section 3.

player.stepPattern.note: The ROM XORs a flag with 1 on every call and steps 1 px when the result is non-zero, 2 px when it is zero — so 1, 2, 1, 2 …, averaging 1.5 px/frame. The flag is cleared whenever the stick is neutral, so the first frame of any new movement is a 1-px step. Do not replace this with its own average: the cadence is the feel.

player.maxShots.note: Two rocket slots in total, whether the fighter is single or dual: the fire handler checks slot 0, then slot 1, then returns. Arcade reference section 3.

player.autoFire.note: The fire handler has no edge detection, so holding the button fires whenever a slot is free. Arcade reference section 3.

player.y.note: The row the fighter sits on. The reference does not give it.

player.width.note: The 16×16 sprite of docs/DESIGN.md section 7.4. The reference gives travel limits in ROM sprite-X bytes but not the fighter’s own box.

player.minX.note: ROM sprite-X `$12`. The ROM’s sprite X is offset from the visible playfield by an amount the reference does not trace, so *the origin* is provisional and is taken as `$12` itself; the geometry pins it to within a pixel, because `$12`…`$E1` is 207 positions of travel that a 16-px fighter turns into 223 of the playfield’s 224 columns — exactly one column goes unvisited whatever the origin, and this choice puts the left limit flush against column 0.

player.maxX.note: ROM sprite-X `$E1`, minus the same origin as player.minX.

player.dualMaxX.note: ROM sprite-X `$D1`, minus the same origin as player.minX.

player.secondShipOffsetX.note: The dual fighter’s second ship is drawn at X + `$0F`.

player.hitWindow.note: Δx ∈ [−6, +6] and Δy ∈ [−3, +3] in the ROM’s half-scaled Y units, so the Y half is doubled here into playfield pixels.

player.respawnFrames.note: Frames the fighter is off the field after a hit. Not in the reference.

player.shot.speed.note: The reference gives no shot speed. Worth knowing that this number *is* the fire rate: with no edge detection and a hard cap of two, how fast shots leave the screen is the only thing deciding how often you may fire again.

player.shot.width.note: Ours; the reference does not give the rocket’s size.

player.shot.muzzleOffsetX.note: Where the muzzle is drawn. Presentation, not a ROM figure.

player.shot.windows.single[0].dxMin.note: A single fighter’s shot tests one window, Δx ∈ [−5, +5]. Arcade reference section 3.

player.shot.windows.single[0].dxMax.note: As the dxMin of the same window.

player.shot.windows.single[0].dyMin.note: The reference does not give the Δy half of any shot window.

player.shot.windows.single[0].dyMax.note: As the dyMin of the same window.

player.shot.windows.dual[0].dxMin.note: A dual fighter’s shot tests two windows, Δx ∈ [−6, +4] and Δx ∈ [+9, +19], with Δx ∈ [+5, +8] deliberately dead. The 15-unit gap between the window centres is the second ship’s `$0F` offset.

player.shot.windows.dual[0].dxMax.note: As the dxMin of the same window.

player.shot.windows.dual[0].dyMin.note: The reference does not give the Δy half of any shot window.

player.shot.windows.dual[0].dyMax.note: As the dyMin of the same window.

player.shot.windows.dual[1].dxMin.note: The second window of the pair; see dual[0].dxMin.

player.shot.windows.dual[1].dxMax.note: As the dxMin of the same window.

player.shot.windows.dual[1].dyMin.note: The reference does not give the Δy half of any shot window.

player.shot.windows.dual[1].dyMax.note: As the dyMin of the same window.

enemies.maxBullets.note: At most eight enemy bullets exist at once, globally rather than per enemy: the routine that creates one searches eight slots and creates nothing when all are taken. Arcade reference section 5.

enemies.bomberReadyTimers.note: Loaded unconditionally at every stage start as `$16`, `$02`, `$02` for the bee, butterfly and boss types. Arcade reference section 7.

enemies.bullet.speed.note: The reference gives no bullet speed.

enemies.bullet.width.note: Ours; the reference does not give the bullet’s size.

enemies.collision.enabled.note: Enemy bodies are lethal to the fighter: [MANUAL] line 1962, quoted in reference section 5 — “if they can’t bomb you, they’ll ram you in the rear”. The window is the fighter’s own player.hitWindow, from the one ROM routine that tests anything against the fighter. What the reference does not settle is whether the ram also destroys the enemy or scores; reference section 11 item 2 records that, and the engine takes the negative reading.

enemies.updatePhases.note: Reference section 2: enemy object state advances on a four-frame round robin at 15 Hz, with the objects split across the four frames. Positions still move every frame; it is the state machine that takes turns.

enemies.dive.baseLaunchRate.note: Ours. The reference gives the per-role launch counters but not the launcher that reads them, so how a counter becomes a cadence is this pack's. It must be positive: rank A stage 1 has all three counters at 0 and the original certainly dives, so a rate of 0 is the floor of the ramp rather than silence.

enemies.dive.launchCost.note: Ours, and the companion to baseLaunchRate: the launcher runs once per four-frame round robin and grants each role baseLaunchRate + its row rate, so 16 makes a rate-0 role try every 64 frames and a rate-8 role every 8. Raising this slows every stage together, which is what keeps it a rule and not a difficulty curve.

enemies.dive.bumpAfterFrames.note: Ours. Reference section 6 confirms parameter 5 "increases allowable max bombers after a time" but does not say how long, so 900 frames — fifteen seconds of diving — is a choice. The two limits either side of it are verified table values.

enemies.dive.returnPath.note: That divers leaving the bottom re-enter from the top and rejoin the formation is confirmed in reference section 5. Which path they fly back is this pack's; that it ends in toSlot is the engine's single homing implementation.

enemies.dive.reentryY.note: One sprite height above the top of the playfield, so the sprite is fully clear when it re-enters. Presentation, not a ROM figure.

enemies.bombing.entryFromStage.note: There is no entry bombing on stage 1; enemies bomb during entry from stage 2 onward. docs/DESIGN.md section 4, and acceptance test R14 of the rules-and-scoring report.

enemies.bombing.vectors.note: That a bomb travels along one of a fixed set of flight vectors rather than along an exactly computed heading is verified in shape (reference section 6 names the bombing flight-vector table and its reload flag) but the table's own headings were never decoded, so these five are ours. They are what makes a bomb dodgeable: an exactly-aimed one dropped from above cannot be side-stepped.

enemies.bombing.altVectors.note: The second table a row's reloadBombVectors swaps in from stage 8. That the swap happens is verified (reference section 6, parameter 9); the headings are ours, and are wider and finer than the first table so the later stages bomb over a broader arc.

enemies.bombing.continuousCooldownFrames.note: Ours. That bombing turns continuous once the live enemy count reaches the row's continuousBombingAt is verified (reference section 6, parameter 7, rising 6 to 12 across rank A); how short "continuous" is, is not in the reference.

transform.types.note: Three types cycling on a four-stage period is verified (reference section 6); the names and the art are this pack's, because docs/DESIGN.md section 2 bars the original's.

transform.fromStage.note: Exactly stage 4. The enabling value is 0 below stage 3 and 0 on a challenge stage, and stage 3 is a challenge stage. Reference section 6, ASM new_stage.s l_2C3F.

transform.remainingThreshold.note: The ROM stores 10 and the transform fires when fewer than 10 enemies remain: f_1A80 returns while the live count is greater than or equal to the threshold. Reference section 6 as corrected by report section 7.6.

transform.stagesPerType.note: The trio type cycles on a four-stage period: stages 4-6, 8-10, 12-14, then repeating. Reference section 6 and MANUAL lines 1892-1898.

transform.groupSize.note: "Special attack squadrons made up of three ships each". MANUAL line 1892.

transform.fromRoles.note: A bee, or a butterfly if no bees remain — the ROM takes the first bee-role object in STAND_BY and falls back to the butterfly-role objects. Reference section 6, LIST main $1A95-$1AAE.

transform.perStage.note: Once per stage: the task disables itself after launching the group. Reference section 6, LIST main $1B5B.

transform.tellFrames.note: That the enemy pulses between two colours before transforming is confirmed (reference section 6, a countdown alternating colour every 16 ticks), but the reference's $C0 byte and its "64 ticks" reading disagree on the length, so 64 frames is ours.

formation.sway.note: Reference section 5, f_2A90: 1 px every 4 frames, a triangle reversing at ±32 px — exactly the margin between the 160 px formation and the 224 px playfield, which is why the sway just touches each edge.

formation.breathe.steps.note: Reference section 5, f_1DE6: 32 steps out and 32 back, one step every 4 frames — a 256-frame cycle.

formation.breathe.stepFrames.note: Reference section 5: the same 15 Hz task rate as the sway, on the opposite phase of the same 4-frame counter.

formation.breathe.columns.note: Reference section 5: 32/25/18/11/4 px outward per column pair, signed here so the left half moves left. The ramp between rest and full expansion is ours — the ROM’s selection bitmaps are ROM data, which docs/DESIGN.md section 2 bars copying — but the totals, and so the positions at rest and at full expansion, are the verified ones.

formation.breathe.rows.note: Reference section 5: 0/4/11/18/25/32 px downward per row, captured-fighter row first and never moving.

formation.animatedStageKinds.note: Reference section 5: neither motion runs on a challenge stage, because nothing settles into formation there, so f_2A90 never reaches the exit that enables the breathe.

capture.captorRole.note: Only the boss role captures: the tractor-beam boss is the capture channel's only actor, and it brings no escorts. Reference section 7.

capture.divePath.note: The shape is described but not measured: a capture boss loops once at the top of the formation, slides down to roughly mid-screen and emits the beam (reference section 7, which rates the descent depth High and notes its two sources disagree). So the geometry is ours, and the beam comes out at the path's own captureBeam trigger rather than at a depth the engine knows.

capture.captiveAlien.note: That a captured fighter becomes a red ship in the formation which attacks, can be shot for 500/1,000 and re-enters with the next stage's wave is verified (reference section 7); the alien document, its dive path and its art are this pack's, because docs/DESIGN.md section 2 bars the original's.

capture.everyNthLaunch.note: Only every second eligible boss launch may be a capture boss: the ROM pre-increments a counter and tests its low bit, which is also why the first boss launch of a game never carries a beam. Reference section 7, LIST main $1C0D.

capture.maxHeldTotal.note: Exactly one captured fighter, globally, ever. The flag is set the instant a capture boss is selected and a successful capture does not clear it, so no second attempt happens while one is held — including while it is parked as a rogue — and a dual fighter is never targeted. Reference section 7; the rules-and-scoring report section 3.2 enumerated every write to the flag's byte.

capture.lastFighterCaptureEndsGame.note: “When the enemy destroys or captures your last fighter, the words GAME OVER are displayed”. A loss condition distinct from being shot, and one docs/DESIGN.md originally missed. Reference section 7, MANUAL line 1972.

capture.disablesFireWhileBeamed.note: Once the boss has connected with the ship the player's fire is disabled — the ROM routine is named for it. Reference section 7, ASM gg1-3.s l_214C_disable_firepower.

capture.beam.steps.note: That the beam extends one animation step per period is verified (reference section 6, parameter 6); how many steps it takes is not in the reference, so 8 is ours. The period itself is a verified table value and is read from the difficulty row.

capture.beam.holdSteps.note: How long the beam stays fully extended before retracting. Ours: the reference records only that it retracts when the player is not in range.

capture.beam.catchWindow.note: The beam's catch geometry. The reference gives no beam width or reach, so these are ours, chosen so a beam opened at the descent depth capture.divePath reaches does get down to the fighter's row. Its dyMax is scaled by how far the beam has extended, which is what makes a slow early beam escapable.

capture.carrySteps.note: How many beam steps the pull-in takes. Ours; that the pull is paced by the same countdown as the extension is the reference's (“the beam extends and pulls four times faster by stage 20”, section 6, parameter 6), which is why this is counted in steps rather than frames.

capture.rogueDelayFrames.note: How long a rogue fighter sits in its slot before it swoops. The reference says only “eventually” (section 7), so 240 frames is ours. It is what makes parking a rogue a technique: there is time to shoot it in formation for 500 instead of 1,000.

rescue.requiresCaptorAttacking.note: The rescue needs the boss destroyed “while they are both attacking your current fighter”, and the ROM takes the branch only when the captured ship's status is the diving state. Reference section 7, MANUAL line 1869 and ASM gg1-5.s cp #9.

rescue.freedShipInvulnerableWhileDocking.note: The freed fighter spins in mid-space and cannot be destroyed until it joins you. Reference section 7 rates the detail High and names the corroborating ROM task flag, “capturing boss destroyed, rescued ship spinning”, which the rocket manager reads to change hit detection.

rescue.divingEnemiesReturnToFormation.note: Enemies already in mid-dive return to formation at the moment of a rescue. Reference section 7 rates this High, from the same ROM task flag as the invulnerability.

rescue.dockFrames.note: How long the freed fighter spins before it docks as the second ship. Ours; the reference describes the spin but gives no length.

dualFighter.bulletsPerShot.note: One logical shot, two bullets: the rocket gets the hardware double-width attribute from the two-ship flag, so the cap stays at two shots and each is drawn as two. Reference section 3.

dualFighter.losingHalfCostsLife.note: That a hit on either half leaves a single ship is verified (reference section 7) and that losing a half releases the capture channel is ROM-traced (report section 3.2, LIST sub $0610/$0628); that the reserve is untouched is our reading of it, since the ship in play was never lost. Making it a rule rather than an assumption is the difference between a rescue being worth a life and being worth nothing.

challengeStages.firstStage.note: The ROM’s own test is `(stage + 1) mod 4 == 0`, so the first challenge stage is 3. Arcade reference section 8.

challengeStages.everyStages.note: And then every fourth stage — 7, 11, 15 … — from the same test. Arcade reference section 8 also records why the operator manual’s “every third STAGE” reads otherwise.

scoring.movingMultiplier.note: A target that is neither at home in the formation nor rotating back into its slot scores exactly twice its formation value; the ROM stashes the test at `$078D` and consumes it at `$080D`. Arcade reference section 9.

scoring.escortBonus.note: `d_1CFD` = {13, 5, 1} units of 100 indexed by escort count, added to a captor's doubled 300 to give 1,600 / 800 / 400. Latched at launch and reset to the solo entry at every stage start — the per-boss record `bmbr_boss_scode` is written in exactly two places and nothing updates it when an escort dies, so killing the escorts first does not reduce the captor's value. Arcade reference section 9.

scoring.transformGroupBonus.note: `d_1B59` = {30, 10, 20} units of 100 selected by `(floor(stage / 4) mod 3) + 4`, which is 1,000 at stage 4, 2,000 at 8, 3,000 at 12 and 1,000 again at 16 — a rule rather than a table of stage bands. Arcade reference section 6.

scoring.challenge.groupBonus.note: `d_stage_chllg_rnd_attrib` = {10, 15, 20, 30} units of 100, indexed `(stage >> 3) AND 3` and clamped to 3 from stage 32 — 1,000 / 1,000 / 1,500 / 1,500 / 2,000 / 2,000 / 3,000 by challenge-stage ordinal, then held. Arcade reference section 8.

scoring.challenge.perHit.note: 100 × the number of hits, awarded once at the end of the stage. Arcade reference section 8, `gctl_chllng_stg_end`.

scoring.challenge.perfect.note: A flat 10,000 for all 40. Arcade reference section 8.

scoring.challenge.perfectReplacesPerHit.note: The perfect branch loads 100 units and the ordinary branch loads the hit count; both join the same adder, so they are mutually exclusive. Adding them instead is 4,000 points too many on every perfect stage. Arcade reference section 8.

scoring.challenge.impactAward.note: Every hit scores at the moment of impact, at the enemy’s score group doubled — and each challenge stage overwrites every enemy’s score group from `d_290E`, indexed `(stage >> 2) AND 7` with no clamp. So 100 on the 1st challenge stage, 160 on the 2nd–8th, and 100 again on the 9th as the index wraps while the group bonus stays clamped. The table cycles rather than plateauing for exactly that reason. Arcade reference section 8.

starfield.speed.note: The ROM computes `$40 + ((min(stage, 16) × 4) AND $70)` at the start of every stage, giving the five bytes `$40 $50 $60 $70 $80`, one step every four stages, plateauing from stage 16. The byte is a hardware register shadow, not a pixel rate. The conversion is closed too and is `byte / 64`, dithered to whole pixels by the ROM's six-bit phase accumulator, but it is presentation and so lives in src/render/starfield.ts rather than here.
